Title: Operationalizing Responsible AI in High-Stakes Contexts
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    Operationalizing Responsible AI in High-Stakes Contexts    Date & Time:  07 July 2026, 14:15–15:00 CEST    Organizers:  University College London (UCL)     Background and focus  This side event addresses a critical governance gap: the disconnect between high-level AI  governance principles and their translation into situated practice in data-sensitive, multi- stakeholder environments such as humanitarian response. Existing risk-centric approaches to AI  governance emphasise technical failures – hallucinations, security vulnerabilities, adversarial  attacks – while underplaying misalignments between developers, operational agencies, and  affected communities over what counts as “safe enough,” who is accountable, and whether AI  tools entrench structural inequalities.  Drawing on the concept of AI responsibility rifts (AIRRs), the session will examine how governance  gaps manifest acutely in humanitarian and crisis-affected settings, where AI tools shape  decisions about who receives aid or information, yet those most affected have the least influence  over their design and governance. AIRRs name the specific points of disagreement between  developers, operational agencies, and affected communities that risk-based frameworks alone  fail to surface.   The event showcases AIRR-sensitive approaches, from project-level diagnostics to reference  models for UN-level governance discussions. It brings together practitioners already applying this  lens in the field to highlight the importance of governance approaches that are sensitive to local  realities and centered on the lived experience of those affected by AI systems.    Speakers and Format  Format: a moderated panel discussion followed by audience Q&A  Speakers:  • Shivaang Sharma – Assistant Professor (Lecturer) in Innovation and Entrepreneurship at  the UCL Global Business School for Health   • Madigan Johnson – Head of Communications at Data Friendly Space  • Brent Phillips – Founder at Humanitarian AI Today  • Valentin Pistorozzi – Founder at BoldCode_    The session will open with a short framing presentation from Dr. Shivaang Sharma introducing AI  responsibility rifts (AIRRs), followed by a panel discussion in which speakers from organisations in  the humanitarian sector examine how the AIRRs lens has surfaced disagreements between  developers, humanitarian agencies, and affected communities in their own work, and how it has  helped prioritise governance interventions. The format is designed to foreground practitioner  experience from across the humanitarian AI ecosystem rather than a traditional presentation-only  format. The final portion will invite audience Q&A and focus on identifying concrete next steps for  embedding AIRR-sensitive governance within global practices.    Focal Point/Contact:  Elise Pi, Policy Adviser, UCL Policy Impact Unit  elise.pi@ucl.ac.uk

text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva Human-Centred AI Governance: Bridging Skills, Ethics, Inclusion and the  Future of Work Date & Time: 7 July 2026, 13:30–14:15 Geneva CEST | (45-minute online side event) Organiser: Academy Achievers (#BeMeDigitalInclusion) Artificial intelligence is reshaping every sector of society, making inclusive and human- centred governance more important than ever. This interactive keynote explores  practical approaches to AI governance through the lenses of skills development, ethics,  digital inclusion and the future of work, demonstrating how global principles can be  translated into meaningful action across education, industry and communities. Background and focus Artificial intelligence is transforming economies, education systems, labour markets and  public services at an unprecedented pace. While AI presents significant opportunities to  accelerate innovation and sustainable development, it also raises important questions  about governance, ethics, equity, workforce transformation and public trust. As  governments and organisations develop AI policies and regulatory frameworks, there is  an increasing need to ensure that implementation remains human-centred, inclusive and  responsive to the needs of diverse communities. This keynote explores how human-centred AI governance can bridge the gap between  global policy discussions and practical implementation. Drawing on experiences from  education, workforce development, digital inclusion and responsible AI initiatives across   the United Kingdom and Africa, the session will examine how governments, educators,  industry and civil society can work together to build AI ecosystems that create  opportunity while protecting human dignity and promoting trust. The keynote will focus on five interconnected themes: responsible AI governance; AI  literacy and skills development; ethics and public trust; digital inclusion; and the future of  work. Particular emphasis will be placed on ensuring women, young people and  underserved communities are not only prepared for an AI-enabled economy but are  actively involved in shaping it. Aligned with the objectives of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance, the session will  encourage international collaboration, knowledge exchange and practical capacity- building. Participants will gain actionable insights that support responsible AI adoption,  strengthen digital capability and contribute to inclusive, resilient and trusted AI  ecosystems. The discussion also supports broader efforts towards achieving the  Sustainable Development Goals by promoting equitable access to AI opportunities and  ensuring that technological progress benefits society as a whole. Speakers and Format Format: 45-minute interactive online keynote presentation followed by moderated  audience discussion. Speaker: Paulette Watson MBE – Founder and Managing Director, Academy Achievers;  Global Lead, #BeMeDigitalInclusion. Paulette Watson MBE is an AI governance advisor, educator, author and international  speaker whose work focuses on responsible AI, digital inclusion, STEM education and  workforce transformation across the United Kingdom and Africa. Through Academy  Achievers and the #BeMeDigitalInclusion initiative, she collaborates with governments,  educational institutions, industry and community organisations to expand equitable  access to digital skills and support human-centred approaches to AI adoption. The keynote will explore practical strategies for translating AI governance principles into  action through education, workforce development and inclusive innovation. Drawing on  cross-sector experience and international collaboration, the presentation will  demonstrate how responsible AI can strengthen public trust, expand participation and  prepare communities for the future of work.  The final part of the session will be dedicated to audience questions and discussion,  encouraging participants to exchange perspectives, identify shared challenges and  explore practical actions that advance responsible, inclusive and human-centred AI  governance across regions and sectors. She has contributed to responsible AI and digital inclusion initiatives across the UK and  Africa and regularly advises organisations on human-centred AI, workforce  transformation and digital skills. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva Workshop on “Equity Lens: AI Guardrails for Fair Talent Selection,  Recognition, and Opportunity” Date & Time:  Monday, 6 July 2026 | 14:00–14:45 CEST Organizers:  Working Group on Equal Opportunities (AKC) of the German Physical Society (DPG) Co-organizer: Sumiko Shimo, Expert member of UNESCO AI Ethics without Borders &  Women for Ethical AI, G20 Technical Facility, ISO/IEC SC42 on AI Contributors:  Dr. Iris Traulsen, AIP Leibniz Institute for Astrophysics Potsdam Sebastian Dohrmann, German Physical Society Background and focus As AI becomes part of institutional decision-making, including decisions about selection,  recognition, funding, leadership opportunities, and career advancement, governance  frameworks must ensure that these systems do not reproduce existing inequities. Many  selection processes are already shaped by unconscious bias and structural patterns that  are difficult to detect, such as reliance on familiar names, concentration within certain  institutions or networks, repeat visibility, and unequal assessment across career stages.  Equity Lens responds to this challenge by exploring how AI-supported transparency  mechanisms can help make such patterns visible before decisions are finalized. This workshop invites participants to co-design the next stage of Equity Lens, a prototype  transparency tool designed to support fairer, more evidence-based selection processes.  Rather than automating decisions or replacing human judgment, Equity Lens provides  privacy-preserving, aggregated indicators of potential structural bias before committees   reach final decisions. The tool does not rank candidates, recommend outcomes, collect  individual votes, or influence committee choices. Its purpose is to help decision-makers  recognize patterns that might otherwise remain invisible, support informed reflection, and  keep responsibility firmly with human decision-makers. This session is for participants who want to help turn AI governance principles into  practical tools for fairer decision-making. Participants will test the Equity Lens concept,  share concerns and use cases from their own sectors, and help define the requirements,  safeguards, and design priorities for an open-source version of the tool. By joining,  participants can contribute directly to a practical requirements specification and help  shape an approach that organizations with different levels of technical capacity could  adapt for responsible, rights-respecting selection processes. Speakers and Format Format: Interactive co-creation workshop This workshop brings together perspectives from scientific practice, equality initiatives, AI  ethics,  standardization,  and  responsible  technology  governance.  It  moves  beyond  knowledge exchange toward developing practical requirements for ethical transparency  tools. Provisional speakers: Ruzin Aganoglu, PhD – Physicist, CTO of Lab-on-Fiber GmbH, and Deputy Spokesperson of  the Working Group on Equal Opportunities (AKC) of the German Physical Society (DPG). She  advances equity initiatives in physics, promotes STEM role models, and builds national and  international networks. She will provide a science–industry innovation perspective and  introduce practical challenges from research communities and professional societies that  motivated Equity Lens. Sumiko Shimo  – Independent researcher and expert member of UNESCO AI Ethics  Without  Borders,  Women4Ethical  AI,  the  G20  Technical  Facility,  ISO  SC42  on  AI  standardization, and CAIDP. She specializes in responsible AI, ethical innovation, bias  mitigation, and inclusive technology governance. She will facilitate ethical reflection,  connecting  Equity  Lens  with  principles  of  fairness,  transparency,  privacy  protection,  accountability, and human oversight. Agenda: 5 min – Introduction and context 10 min – Prototype demonstration and roadmap  20 min – Discussion and feedback 10 min – Next steps The workshop will deliver a stakeholder-informed framework defining ethical principles,  governance safeguards, and technical requirements for transparent selection processes. Focal Point/Contact: Dr. Ruzin Aganoglu Deputy Spokesperson Working Group on Equal Opportunities (AKC) of the German Physical Society (DPG) Email: ruzin.aganoglu@lab-on-fiber.de

Title: A Common Language for AI Governance: An Open Vocabulary and
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva A Common Language for AI Governance: An Open Vocabulary and  Toolkit for Multistakeholder Adoption Across Spheres of Influence Date & Time:  Tuesday, 7 July 2026, 12:00–12:45 CEST (online side event) Organizers:  AI Integrity Organization (AIO), Geneva, Switzerland Background and focus AI governance increasingly depends on a shared understanding of what AI systems  actually prioritise, yet policymakers, regulators, domain professionals and civil-society  actors still describe AI behaviour in different and often incompatible vocabularies —  “bias,” “fairness,” “alignment,” “trustworthiness.” Without a common, measurable  reference point, multistakeholder cooperation remains principled in intent but  fragmented in practice. This session introduces an open, MIT-licensed vocabulary and toolkit that any  stakeholder can adopt without specialised technical training. It is grounded in Schwartz  basic-values theory — validated across more than 80 cultures — and operationalised  through 366,120 forced-choice measurements across eight commercial AI models in  seven professional domains (S. Lee, 2026b; arXiv:2604.11216). Three findings frame the  policy stakes: the models reverse their value priorities in 37–50% of cases when the same  dilemma is reframed from another stakeholder’s perspective; all eight restructure their  value hierarchies in defence contexts, with Security surging to dominance; and in  education several prioritise institutional compliance over learner self-direction at rates  above 85%. AI systems, in short, do not hold stable value commitments — a foundational   challenge for any governance framework that assumes transparent, predictable  reasoning. The evidence is paired with the AIO 20002 logging standard, an open-source instrument  that maps AI reasoning to structured value/evidence/source codes designed to support  the reasoning-traceability goals of EU AI Act Articles 12–14 (a voluntary instrument, not a  certified compliance mechanism) and deployable today, ahead of the Act’s 2 August 2026  milestones. The session speaks directly to the cluster on Safe, secure and trustworthy AI:  interoperability and compatibility of approaches, while lowering the technical-fluency  barrier that keeps non-technical voices out of AI-governance debate. By giving every  participant a concrete, shared reference for what a model prioritised and why, it turns  multistakeholder collaboration from a stated principle into a working method each actor  can apply within their own sphere of influence. Speakers and Format Format (45 minutes, online).  The session pairs a short evidence briefing with two interactive instruments used for  outcome measurement rather than decoration. Opening (3 min) frames the core  message and a sphere-of-influence matrix.  Part 1 — The Shared Vocabulary (12 min), delivered by Seulki Lee, Founder of the AI  Integrity Organization (Geneva), presents the empirical findings and the vocabulary chain  from Schwartz values to the Authority Stack model to the AIO 20002 logging standard. Part 2 — Bring It Home (10 min) runs a live clinical-scenario poll, compares audience  judgement with measured AI behaviour, and demonstrates AIO 20002 logging. Part 3 —  Govern AI From Your Seat (15 min) is a moderated roundtable of invited international  experts spanning regulatory compliance (Europe), AI security and governance (Africa),  and applied AI evaluation (Asia-Pacific), each showing how the vocabulary applies in their  sphere of influence. A closing segment (5 min) captures adoption-intent polling and  follow-up. Participants leave with three free, ready-to-use assets — a Vocabulary Reference Card, a  one-page “Get Started in Your Sphere” guide, and an open Call for Co-authors to the AIO  Working Paper Series — and AIO will share a multistakeholder synthesis report with the  Joint Secretariat after the event.  Focal Point/Contact:  Seulki Lee, Founder & CEO, AI Integrity Organization (AIO) — 2sk@aioq.org — aioq.org

text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva Comparing National AI-in-Education Policy Approaches: Towards  Building a Shared Framework Date & Time:  7 July 2026, 12:30–13:30 CEST  Organizers: UNESCO Link: Online, via Zoom Background and focus Artificial intelligence (AI) has an increasing presence in all facets of education,  challenging the fundamental assumptions about the role of education to develop the  knowledge, skills and confidence needed to participate fully in society. In view of the  rapid shifts associated with this technology, many governments have shown interest in  developing coherent national policies for AI in education, but may lack institutional  capacity, technical expertise, and contextual evidence to create a workable strategy.  In this context, this session will look to build on the shared foundation set by UNESCO’s  Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research and its twin AI Competency Framework  for Teachers and AI Competency Framework for Students while seeking to deepen  understanding of the ways in which policy and practice around AI in education converge  and differ across diverse contexts. Offering a rich dialogue between academic experts  and experienced policy-makers, it will surface and compare approaches of education  policy-makers against a common set of dimensions, identifying shared building blocks,  context-specific divergences, and unresolved gaps, with the aim of producing a  comparative mapping that can inform the development of a comprehensive AI in   Education policy framework for Ministries of Education and a complementary tool to  assess ‘readiness’, building upon existing UNESCO guidance. Title: “Making AI Data Work Accountable: The Fairwork Certification Scheme”
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva “Making AI Data Work Accountable: The Fairwork Certification Scheme” Date & Time:  Tue 7 July 2026 12:45–13:30 CEST Organizers:  Fairwork, Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford Background and focus (300 words) AI systems rely on hidden human labour in tasks like data annotation, model evaluation,  content review, and moderation, often through complex supply chains that pose  documented labour risks like low pay, insecure contracts, intense productivity  monitoring, and exposure to distressing content, with poor worker access to remedy. Considering strengthened regulations like the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Due  Diligence Directive (CS3D) or California’s Assembly Bill 2653, firms developing or  implementing AI systems face reputational, legal, and operational risks because most  companies still lack an assurance mechanism for labour due diligence in AI supply  chains. Fairwork can help companies navigate new regulations, avoid reputational  damage, prevent operational disruptions, and improve working conditions. In this lightning talk, we will introduce the Fairwork Certification Scheme as a governance  framework for improving labour conditions and accountability in AI data work. By  presenting the rationale and structure of the Fairwork certification scheme, the session  explores how evidence-based standards can address opacity and fragmented  responsibility within AI production networks to inform corporate due diligence  mechanisms. After the presentation, the session invites the audience to reflect on  practical pathways for implementing labour governance.  It contributes to the Global Dialogue on AI Governance by advancing human-rights- based approaches to transparent, trustworthy, and inclusive AI governance.  Speakers and Format (200 words) The presentation will be hosted by Shilpa Mariam Joseph, a research assistant at the  Fairwork project. Title: Who Governs AI in Practice? Women's Agency, Accountability and Human
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva  Who Governs AI in Practice? Women's Agency, Accountability and Human  Oversight    Date & Time:  07 July 2026, 13:00–13:45 CEST.    Organizers: Connecting Women in Digital (WIDCON) / Women in Digital Forum – Thematic Working  Group 6, chaired by Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya · BarcelonaTech (UPC).    Background and focus   The session is proposed by Connecting Women in Digital (WIDCON) / Women in Digital Forum –  Thematic Working Group 6, which brings together experts from policy, legal, technical, private-sector,  research and organisational governance backgrounds. The virtual format is intentional, supporting  accessible and cross-regional participation while reducing barriers to engagement.  The proposal builds on TWG6’s work on women’s agency in the AI economy, organisational AI  governance, human oversight, workforce impact assessment, transparency, accountability and  capacity-building. It reflects a shared recognition that trustworthy and inclusive AI governance requires  more than high-level principles. Effective implementation depends on clear organisational accountability  structures: who approves AI use cases, who monitors impacts, who exercises human oversight, who  escalates concerns, and how affected groups, including women, are represented in governance and  decision-making processes.  Particular attention will be given to the practical challenge of operationalising accountability across  complex organisational environments, where responsibilities are often distributed across legal,  compliance, technical, business, HR and management functions. The session will connect AI  governance principles with measurable implementation mechanisms, including operational  transparency, gender-responsive indicators, evidence-based monitoring, CSR and sustainability  governance links, workforce impact assessment and board-level accountability.  The discussion will also explore the conditions under which women move from being affected by AI- driven change to actively shaping how AI is built, adopted and governed. This includes organisational  factors such as leadership behaviour, access to learning opportunities, meaningful participation in AI- related decisions and capacity-building.   By bringing together European governance practitioners, policy experts and Global South and Latin  American perspectives, the session will identify practical approaches for embedding accountability,  inclusion and human oversight into AI governance frameworks. The discussion connects to SDGs 5, 8, 9,  10 and 16 by linking women’s agency, decent work, inclusive innovation, reduced inequalities and  accountable institutions.  A short takeaway note will capture cross-regional insights and practical recommendations on gender- responsive AI governance.    Speakers and Format   The proposed 45-minute virtual side event will focus on how women move from being affected by AI to  shaping AI governance in practice. Ruth Martínez-López, TWG6 Chair, with Ilker Demirkol as Co-Chair if  available, will open with a 3-minute framing of WIDCON/TWG6 and the core governance challenge.  The core panel will include three short expert inputs. Georgia Voudoulaki will address operational AI  governance, institutional accountability, human oversight and responsibility structures. Catherine  Mulligan will connect AI labour-market transformation, just transition, women as builders of AI, digital  skills, adoption and decent work. Ciara O’Buachalla and Rania Souhlal will provide a joint contribution:  Ciara on private-sector implementation and AI compliance ownership across legal, HR, IT, compliance  and business functions; Rania on gender-responsive KPIs, double materiality, cross-functional escalation  risks, Board and C-suite decision-making, and auditable evidence architecture.  A brief guided exchange with Fadima Diawara, facilitated by Caroline De Cock, will bring a Francophone  Africa perspective on digital inclusion, capacity-building and implementation constraints.  The session will then move to a 10-minute moderated discussion led by Mara Saenger with Gabriela  Arriagada-Bruneau and Polona Pičman Štefančič, adding Latin American, data-sovereignty, human-rights  and Caribbean perspectives. The session will close with 5 minutes of practical takeaways and next steps.    Focal Point/Contact:  Ruth Martinez Lopez (ruth.martinez.lopez@upc.edu)

Title: Building Technical Sovereignty: AI Safety and Security Capacity as a
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva Building Technical Sovereignty: AI Safety and Security Capacity as a  Governance Foundation in the Global South Date & Time:  06 July 2026, 18:00–19:00 CEST Organizers: Asuntos del Sur  Access link: https://us06web.zoom.us/j/83211211214? pwd=kzuNaOZKXV21bMd0RsiGRNYlZlzZbc.1 Background and focus Technical sovereignty in AI rests on a country's or region's actual capacity to understand, audit,  red-team, and govern the AI systems it deploys and depends on. For most of the Global South,  building this capacity is the central condition for participating in AI governance as an active agent,  with real influence over the standards that get set. Co-organised by Asuntos del Sur and the Global Council for Responsible AI, this session brings  together practitioners working on the ground in Latin America and Africa to examine what building  this capacity actually requires: AI safety literacy for policymakers and civil society, security  standards and red-teaming practices adapted to local threat landscapes, privacy-preserving  infrastructure that keeps data and models under domestic or regional control, and governance  frameworks grounded in local realities. The session focuses on concrete, transferable practices: how edge-AI and privacy-enhancing  computation can strengthen domestic control over cloud infrastructure; how AI red-teaming and  security operations expertise can be grown regionally; and how ambassador and chapter-based  networks can translate global governance debates into local policy influence. The panel will also  address the specific barriers Global South institutions face — talent retention, funding models,  and limited input into the technical standards that get set globally — and identify forms of South- South cooperation that could accelerate progress on these gaps.  The goal is to ground the conversation on AI governance in the Global South in the technical and  institutional foundations that make governance principles enforceable in practice. The session  aims to produce concrete takeaways for the Global Dialogue on how safety and security capacity  building should be prioritised and resourced going forward. Speakers and Format This is a moderated panel discussion, followed by open Q&A with the audience. text_string: Concept note     Beyond Algorithms: Youth Voices Shaping the Future of Ethical AI  Governance  Background and Focus (~300 words)  Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming societies across the world,  influencing how people learn, work, communicate, and access essential  services. From automated decision-making systems to generative AI  tools, these technologies are increasingly embedded in daily life and  public infrastructure. While AI brings significant opportunities for  innovation and efficiency, it also raises urgent ethical and governance  challenges, including algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns,  misinformation, surveillance risks, and unequal access to digital  technologies.  As AI systems become more powerful and autonomous, decisions that  affect individuals and communities are often shaped by systems that lack  transparency or accountability. Despite being among the most impacted  by these technologies, young people are frequently excluded from  formal discussions on AI governance and policy design. This exclusion  creates a critical gap in representation and limits the development of  inclusive, human-centered digital futures.  This session, led by Brave Voices, aims to address this gap by centering  youth voices in global conversations on ethical AI governance. It   explores how young people can meaningfully participate in shaping  responsible, transparent, and rights-based AI systems.  The discussion will focus on key themes such as algorithmic fairness  and bias, digital rights and safety, transparency in AI decision-making,  and accountability mechanisms for emerging technologies. It will also  explore the impact of AI-driven systems on youth participation in civic  spaces, education, and access to information.  By bringing together youth leaders from diverse backgrounds, the  session promotes the idea that ethical AI governance must be inclusive,  participatory, and grounded in human rights. It emphasizes that young  people are not only users of technology but essential stakeholders in  shaping its future. The goal is to empower youth to actively contribute to  policy discussions and co-create equitable digital systems that reflect the  needs of all generations. text_string: AI Accountability in Practice: Financial  Standards, Compliance and Operational  Guardrails Organizers 1. Pride AI and Business Solutions (prideaiandbusinesssolutions.com) 2. DocsOrb (docsorb.com) Concept Note Part A: Background and Focus AI is becoming core economic and operational infrastructure, but the knowledge gap on AI  Governance is not up to speed. Financial institutions and regulators still lack reliable methods to  assess the real value, defensibility, and downside risk of AI systems. At the same time,  organizations adopting AI tools often rely on static policies, manual reviews, and after-the-fact  audits, leaving data exposure, shadow AI use, and compliance violations unmanaged in real  time. This side-event presents AI accountability through two connected pillars. Financial Accountability via “IFRS for AI”: Pride AI introduces a framework for recognizing  and measuring AI systems as auditable computational assets. It addresses the “capital erasure”  problem in current accounting models, where continuous investment in data, GPU or  engineering is valued through four key pillars: Recognition, Measurement, Disclosure, and  Governance. Through asset manifests, data provenance, defensibility measures, and valuation  models, IFRS for AI aims to help investors, central banks, and sovereign funds distinguish  genuine technical moats from fragile AI wrappers. Operational Enforcement via Policy-to-Guardrail Governance: DocsOrb focuses on how  organizations turn written policies into enforceable AI controls. In most organizations,  compliance, legal, HR, risk, security, and data protection teams define what AI use is allowed,  restricted, or blocked, but enforcement remains manual or technical. DocsOrb bridges that gap  by translating organizational policies into AI guardrails, detecting risky use, preventing sensitive  data exposure, and generating audit evidence. Together, these pillars move AI governance beyond principles. The session explores how AI  can be valued, governed, enforced, and audited through practical frameworks that support trust,  compliance, cybersecurity, and institutional accountability.  Part B: Speakers ● Tamiru Belayneh Hassen (Founder & CEO, Pride AI and Business Solutions;  Google Cloud Partner): Tamiru works at the intersection of finance, technology,  transformation, and governance. As Founder and CEO of Pride AI and Business  Solutions, he brings more than 20 years of experience across financial services,  institutional banking, operations, leadership, and regulatory compliance in Ethiopia and  the United States. His work focuses on AI strategy, governance, security, and financial  governance solutions, including the emerging “IFRS for AI” framework for valuing and  reporting AI systems as accountable computational assets. ● Santhosh Komaragiri (Founder & CEO, DocsOrb): Santhosh brings over 8 years of  experience in data privacy, compliance, and cybersecurity, serving mid-market and  enterprise organizations. He surfaces a simple principle: engineers implement controls,  but organizations own the policy. Through DocsOrb, compliance, legal, HR, risk, and  security teams can define what AI use is allowed, restricted, or blocked, while technical  teams implement those decisions with audit evidence. Title: Designed Elsewhere, Deployed Here: How African Institutions Can Lead AI
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva  Designed Elsewhere, Deployed Here: How African Institutions Can Lead AI  Accountability Before It's Imposed Date & Time:  6 July 2026, 07:00–07:45 CEST Organizers:  WINAR Institute for AI Policy and Governance in Africa Background and focus Across East Africa, AI systems increasingly inform decisions with direct consequences for  people's livelihoods: creditworthiness in fintech, triage in healthcare, eligibility in public  administration. The frameworks meant to govern these systems, however, were largely designed  elsewhere. European and American accountability models assume institutional conditions that  do not hold in most African deployment environments: reliable audit infrastructure, dense  regulatory capacity, and mature legal recourse mechanisms. This gap is not theoretical. When an imported governance framework meets an African institution  with fewer resources, thinner audit trails, and different regulatory maturity, the result is often an  accountability vacuum rather than accountability itself. A framework built for a well resourced  regulator does not simply scale down. It fails silently, leaving deployed systems ungoverned in  practice even when a policy exists on paper. This session argues that closing that gap requires two shifts. First, accountability mapping must  happen before deployment, not after harm surfaces, so that responsibility is assigned while a  system is still being designed rather than reconstructed retroactively during a crisis. Second,  contextual validation must be treated as a deployment requirement rather than an optional add  on: a model validated for one institutional environment cannot be assumed safe for another  without testing against local data conditions, local infrastructure constraints, and local  enforcement realities. Drawing on Kenya's AI Bill 2026 and emerging governance practice across East Africa, the session  examines what it looks like for African institutions to move from recipients of AI governance to its  architects, building tools calibrated to low resource institutional environments rather than   adapting frameworks built for different ones. The conversation is not simply about resisting  imported governance. It is about building the accountability infrastructure African institutions  actually need, with African expertise at the centre of designing it. Speakers and Format This session takes the form of a 45 minute fireside chat between Winston Mariku and Ole Gamba,  structured as a direct conversation rather than a formal panel, to allow for genuine exchange on  the realities of AI accountability in African institutional contexts. Winston Mariku is Founder and Chief Executive Director of WINAR Institute for AI Policy and  Governance in Africa, an AI Governance and Strategy Advisor working on accountability  frameworks and contextual validation standards for African organizations deploying AI in finance,  healthcare, and public administration. Ole Gamba brings frontline experience navigating cybersecurity, AI, and digital resilience within  one of Africa's largest technology and telecommunications institutions, Safaricom, offering a  practitioner's view of what governance gaps look like when AI systems are deployed at scale  inside African infrastructure. The conversation moves between framework and frontline: Winston brings the accountability  architecture argument from her UN Global Dialogue submission, while Ole grounds it in the  operational realities of deploying and securing AI systems within a major African institution.  Together, the session examines what it actually takes for African institutions to move from  governance recipients to governance architects, closing with concrete reflections on what  accountability infrastructure needs to look like to survive contact with real deployment  environments. Focal Point/Contact: Winston Mariku, winstonaigovernance@gmail.com

Evidence suggests that large language models in languages other  than English cost more to run, are more likely to fail safety tests and hallucinate  dangerous misinformation. The implications of these asymmetries for multilingualism,  and their implications for the spread of AI opportunities, have become a governance  challenge. Linguistic diversity is crucial to ensure inclusivity of the digital space. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva Intelligence Beyond Borders:  Empowering the Next Billion Toward an AI-Ready, Ethical and Equitable  Future Date & Time:  07 July 2026, 17:30–18:30 CEST  Organizers:  AI and Quantum International Hub (AIQUAINT)  Background and focus Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping labor markets, education systems, and  governance structures worldwide — yet the benefits and risks of this transformation are  not evenly distributed. For the "next billion" digital citizens, largely concentrated across  the Global South, AI presents both a historic opportunity for economic leapfrogging and  a serious risk of deepening existing inequalities. Millions of young people possess the  talent and ambition to shape the AI era, but structural gaps — in infrastructure, digital  literacy, funding, and representation in policy conversations — threaten to leave them as  consumers rather than co-creators of AI systems. This session moves beyond diagnosing the problem to showcasing what is already  working on the ground. Drawing on experience across Asia and the Middle East, the  panel will highlight national youth AI summits, "AI for Good" initiatives, and community- driven education programs that embed ethics and equity into AI literacy from the outset  — rather than treating them as an afterthought. The UAE, as a hub connecting South  Asia, Africa, and the wider Global South, offers a unique vantage point for this discussion,  with speakers bringing direct, cross-regional experience in policy, legal frameworks, and  education.  Central to the conversation is the question of governance: how can young people move  from being subjects of AI policy to genuine participants in shaping it? The panel will  examine mechanisms for embedding youth voice into global AI governance frameworks,  including multilateral dialogues like the UN's own,  o that regulatory and ethical  standards reflect the realities of those who will live longest with AI's consequences. The  session aims to leave participants with concrete models for replication and a clearer  sense of the governance pathways available for youth-led advocacy. Speakers and Format The panel brings together three speakers with complementary expertise and shared  grounding in UAE-based, globally-connected work. Gowri Shankar, Founder of the AI and  Quantum International Hub and an AI Ethicist, brings a technologist's and ethicist's lens  on responsible AI design for emerging economies. Shakilla Jhungeer, Chief Legal and  Compliance Officer at the Global Alliance for Artificial Intelligence (GAFAI), contributes  expertise in international legal and regulatory frameworks governing AI deployment and  accountability. Title: Information Integrity in the Age of AI: Building Trust, Countering
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva Information Integrity in the Age of AI: Building Trust, Countering  Disinformation, and Protecting People Online Date & Time:  Tuesday, 7 July 2026, 07:30–08:15 (45 minutes) Organizers:  Fondation Abeona / Global Trust Challenge, and the European  Broadcasting Union (EBU) Background and focus This session brings together the Global Trust Challenge—a G7-mandated multi- stakeholder coalition building technical and policy tools in information integrity—and the  European Broadcasting Union (EBU) public service media network to address the  systemic erosion of trust across the global information ecosystem. Generative AI is  accelerating both the scale and the sophistication of disinformation while simultaneously  entering the information ecosystem as a direct source audiences consult. Public trust in  news is under sustained pressure: the Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026  (University of Oxford, ~100,000 respondents across 48 markets) found overall news trust  at its lowest point since 2015 (37%), even as AI chatbot use for news reached 10% of  respondents and social media overtook news websites and apps as a news source (54%  vs. 51%). These trends converge with growing concern about AI-enabled harms that fall unevenly  on specific groups, including gendered disinformation and abuse targeting women  (notably women journalists and public figures) and risks to children from AI-generated  content and AI-driven platform design. The UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance  identifies information integrity, transparency, accountability and human rights protection  as core thematic pillars.  The Global Trust Challenge has emerged from the G7 Hiroshima process as a multi-  stakeholder coalition—convened by founding partners including the OECD, IEEE, and  UNESCO, and spearheaded by AI Commons, Fondation Abeona, and others—mandated  to develop information and policy tools to advance information integrity. The Global  Trust Challenge and the EBU each bring complementary, practitioner-level experience to  these questions: one from a multilateral coalition building technical and policy tools for  trust, the other from decades of editorial accountability and audience-trust research  across 68 public service media members in over 50 countries. This session is intended to connect that practitioner experience directly to the Dialogue's  deliberations on safe, secure and trustworthy AI and on human rights protection, ahead  of the Co-Chairs' summary. Speakers and Format Hamdhoon Rashad (Moderator) — Media Project Manager at the EBU, where he  moderates sessions on digital transformation and AI. He recently contributed to a joint  BBC/EBU study on the reliability of AI assistants as news sources. Tanya Perelmuter — Co-Founder of Fondation Abeona and ambassador for the Global  Trust Challenge (GTC), a G7-mandated coalition building trust in the information  infrastructure. Tanya works at the intersection of policy and technology to advance  information integrity, ensure inclusive access to AI, and guarantee that its dividends are  shared equitably and sustainably. Session co-organizer. Luis Jiménez — Head of Business Development & Partnerships at Eurovision News (EBU),  leading collaboration and transformation across Europe's public service media. A former  RTVE Spain journalist and Digital Transformation Expert, he manages the largest  database of public service news content. Session co-organizer. Keita Azuma — Associate Research Fellow at UNU-CRIS, researching media literacy in  the generative AI era and election-integrity cooperation across the Indo-Pacific and EU.  He has served in Japan's Cabinet Secretariat since 2011. Marie-Ève Nadeau — Head of International Affairs at 5Rights Foundation, with a  background in human rights and public policy and a decade advising governments and  civil society on internet governance, online safety, AI, and data protection. Format: moderated panel discussion with a short audience exchange. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva Youth Perspectives on the Social and Ethical Implications of AI in Developing  Countries  Date & Time:  06 July 2026, 08:00–08:30 A.M CEST  Organizers:  Empowered You  Background and focus Artificial  intelligence  is  transforming  education,  employment,  communication  and  social  interaction  worldwide.  For  young  people  in  developing  countries,  AI  presents  significant  opportunities to improve access to knowledge, enhance productivity and foster innovation. At the  same time, it raises important ethical, social and governance challenges, including academic  integrity, workforce disruption, digital inequality, bias and the growing influence of AI on language,  communication and human behaviour. Despite being among the groups most affected by rapid AI adoption, young people in developing  countries remain underrepresented in global AI governance discussions. Their lived experiences  provide valuable insights into how AI is shaping everyday life, highlighting the need for governance  approaches that are inclusive, context-sensitive and responsive to diverse realities. This lightning talk will examine both the opportunities and the implications of AI for young people in  developing countries, encouraging balanced discussion on the benefits of innovation alongside the  need to address emerging risks. Particular attention will be given to transparency, accountability  and meaningful human oversight, while recognising that effective AI governance should support  innovation while safeguarding human rights and promoting responsible use. By bringing a grassroots youth perspective into the Global Dialogue on AI Governance, this session  aims to contribute to ongoing discussions on responsible AI development and use. Participants will  gain insight into the opportunities, challenges and governance considerations surrounding AI in  developing-country contexts, while encouraging greater recognition of youth voices in international  AI governance processes and promoting practical reflection on how AI can remain human-centred,  inclusive and beneficial for all.  Speakers and Format The session will be delivered as a 15-minute lightning talk by the Chair and Founder of  Empowered You, a youth-led initiative focused on youth engagement and AI awareness from a  developing-country perspective. The presentation will explore the opportunities and challenges associated with AI adoption  among young people, covering education, employment, communication, digital inequality and the  evolving relationship between AI and human interaction. Rather than presenting AI solely as either  a solution or a threat, the session will encourage a balanced discussion that considers both the  benefits of innovation and the importance of ethical safeguards, transparency, accountability and  meaningful human oversight. Following the presentation, participants will be invited to contribute questions and brief  reflections, creating an interactive exchange that encourages dialogue among participants from  different regions and stakeholder communities. This flexible format provides an opportunity to  share experiences, compare perspectives and identify common priorities for inclusive,  transparent and human-centred AI governance. The session aims to leave participants with practical insights into how youth perspectives from  developing countries can inform responsible AI development and contribute to more inclusive  international AI governance discussions. Focal Point/Contact: Aggrey Otieno Founder, Empowered You Aggreyotienoowiti@gmailcom

text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva DesertifAI Lightweight Deep Learning for Climate Adaptation in Botswana  and the Global South Date & Time: Tuesday, 7 July 2026, 07:00–08:30 CEST (session expected to run  approximately 30–45 minutes) Organizers: DesertifAI Format: Online session Connection link: https://stanford.zoom.us/j/9713948258? pwd=LZJXx4T7Wspm6WpIKUDalbfyRAQanS.1&omn=93045334043 (Meeting ID: 971  394 8258 | Password: 070726)  Background and focus Climate change and desertification present existential threats to arid and semi-arid  ecosystems, particularly in the Global South. Traditional climate and land- degradation modeling requires immense computational power, often restricting  sophisticated predictive tools to institutions with access to high-performance  supercomputing infrastructure. This creates a severe digital divide, leaving local  policymakers and land managers in highly vulnerable regions without the real- time, high-resolution data necessary for timely environmental intervention and  adaptive management. To address this critical barrier, DesertifAI introduces a paradigm shift in climate  adaptation technology. DesertifAI is an open-source, lightweight AI framework  designed specifically to democratize access to advanced environmental modeling.  By using an optimized, browser-based U-Net operator, the framework accelerates  complex desertification simulations by an unprecedented 5,500 times. This  computational efficiency allows highly detailed, localized predictive models to run  seamlessly on standard consumer hardware - such as basic laptops and tablets -   without requiring supercomputers, specialized local infrastructure, or constant  high-bandwidth internet connectivity. The focus of this session is to showcase the deployment of DesertifAI, drawing  directly from a collaborative partnership with environmental policymakers and  local stakeholders in Botswana. This is generalized to how high-speed, localized AI  can be practically integrated into national climate adaptation policies and regional  land-use planning. Ultimately, this will serve as a scalable roadmap for how  lightweight deep learning can empower local communities, bridge global technical  disparities, and build autonomous climate resilience throughout developing  regions, demonstrating that cutting-edge AI can be successfully deployed under  significant resource constraints. Speakers Aritro Chatterjee is the founder of DesertifAI and a student at Stanford University  studying mathematics, computer science, and earth systems. He develops hybrid  deep-learning and mathematical models to predict desertification and inform  global land-use policy, with research published at IEEE ICDM UGHS, ICML, and  AGU. A Rise Global Fellow, World Science Scholar, and Non-Trivial Fellow, Aritro has  served as one of 25 global UN Youth Parliament members, delivering speeches at  the 78th and 79th UN General Assemblies where he co-drafted the Youth Stimulus  to Deliver Agenda. He is also the founder of The Eco-Perspectives Podcast, which  amplifies youth-led environmental initiatives across seven countries. In this session, Aritro will draw on his technical and policy background to  demonstrate how rigorous computational science can be bridged with institutional  framework design. He will guide attendees through the browser-based U-Net  operator framework, discuss practical policy integration based on collaborative  efforts with stakeholders in Botswana, and share scalable pathways to build  climate-resilient health systems and land-use policies for the world's most  vulnerable communities.

text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva  Proof-of-Emotion:  Cryptographic Sovereignty and Human Authenticity in  Layer-1 Symbiotic Governance Date & Time:  Tuesday, 7 July 2026, 08:15–08:45 CEST (Room K) Organizers:  SASOK Foundation & Evorin LLC Background and focus As artificial intelligence transitions from narrow applications to multi-agent autonomous systems,  the frontier of global governance faces an unprecedented paradigm shift. Traditional  cryptographic identity verification frameworks fail to distinguish between human-generated  keystrokes and sophisticated AI-driven behavioral synthetics. This vulnerability threatens to  undermine democratic consensus, financial sovereignty, and digital trust architectures. The SASOK Foundation introduces "Proof-of-Emotion" (PoE), a pioneering decentralized protocol  built on Layer-1 symbiotic infrastructure. Designed to meet the foundational pillars of UNGA  Resolution A/RES/79/325 and the Global Digital Compact, PoE bridges the gap between raw  compute power and verifiable biological human intent. Unlike invasive biometric tracking, PoE  relies on Zero-Knowledge (ZK) cryptographic proofs that analyze micro-behavioral, non-invasive  cognitive and affective telemetry. This ensures that personal sovereignty and human rights are  fully preserved while maintaining absolute privacy. This side event focuses on the practical implementation of PoE within the context of the AI Act  Conformity Check frameworks. It presents a modular architecture where human authenticity can  be verified on-chain natively, neutralizing deepfake manipulation and automated Sybil attacks at  the infrastructure level. By anchoring technological policy into algorithmic consensus, Layer-1  symbiotic governance provides nations with a scalable, neutral environment to coordinate cross-  border AI safety standards, protect sovereign data integrity, and guarantee human-centric  systemic resilience in an era dominated by synthetic intelligence. Speakers and Format The session will follow an intensive, high-impact Briefing and Technology Demonstration format  (30 minutes), structured to provide both high-level geopolitical insights and concrete engineering  solutions: ●Opening & Problem Definition (5 mins): Contextualizing the erosion of digital human  authenticity under autonomous AI agent deployment. ●Keynote Address (10 mins): Teymur Safiulov, Lead Symbiotic Architect (SASOK  Foundation / Evorin LLC). Presentation of the Layer-1 Symbiotic Governance Whitepaper  and the underlying mathematics of Proof-of-Emotion protocols. ●Live Prototype & Architectural Review (10 mins): Technical deep-dive into ZK-telemetry  validation pipelines, showcasing real-time mitigation of deepfake vectors and automated  coordination threat models within compliant European AI Act infrastructures. ●Interactive Panel Q&A & Policy Synthesis (5 mins): Open floor discussion with delegates  regarding cross-border deployment, sovereign compliance, and strategic integration into  UN-Habitat and ITU global frameworks. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva AI and Job Creation Title: AI and Job Creation Date & Time:  7 July 2026, 07:00 AM – 08:30 AM CEST Organizers:  Lead Entity: Internet Governance Forum (IGF) - Dynamic Coalition on Digital  Economy and Project CREATE                             Co-Organizer: Health Parliament Joining Link: https://zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_CY1nM3loQo2Ji0HjxAjV5w  A short description (2–3 sentences) for the public programme listing:  AI and Job  Creation organized by Internet Governance Forum (IGF) - Dynamic Coalition on Digital Economy,  Project CREATE and Health Parliament examine how artificial intelligence is reshaping labour  markets, displacing routine roles while generating new categories of work and what this means for  workers, economies, and societies. The session brings together policymakers, industry leaders,  and civil society to explore workforce transition strategies, reskilling frameworks, and inclusive  governance design. It calls for co-developed frameworks that ensure AI-driven growth benefits all  workers, not just capital holders. Background and focus Artificial intelligence is no longer a distant technological prospect, it is actively reshaping labour  markets across the world, transforming the nature of work at a pace that public policy, education  systems, and social protection frameworks have yet to match. While AI is displacing routine and  repetitive roles across sectors, it is simultaneously generating entirely new categories of work that  demand new competencies, new institutional arrangements, and new governance approaches.  The central challenge of our time is not whether AI will change work, it will and it already has, but  whether this transformation will be managed in a way that is fair, inclusive, and equitable. History  has shown that technological transitions, when left ungoverned, tend to concentrate gains among  capital holders while distributing costs among workers. The AI transition risks following the same  pattern unless deliberate action is taken by governments, industry, and civil society working  together. The Global Dialogue on AI Governance, convened by the United Nations, represents a historic  opportunity to establish the foundational frameworks that will govern AI's role in economies and  societies. The session on AI and Job Creation sits at the heart of this agenda, addressing the human  dimension of AI deployment; the workers, communities, and institutions most affected by this  transition. Organized by the Internet Governance Forum's Dynamic Coalition on Digital Economy, Project  CREATE (Collaborate to Realize Employment & Entrepreneurship For All Through Technology  Ecosystem), and Health Parliament, this session brings together leading voices from policy,  industry, and civil society to examine workforce transition strategies, reskilling frameworks, and  inclusive policy design. The session urges co-development of governance frameworks that ensure  AI-driven growth benefits all workers, not just capital holders, and advances the vision of Internet  for All and Livelihood for All. Each speaker will be invited to share their perspective for 7-8 minutes,  followed by a moderated discussion and an open Q&A segment. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6-7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva Pathways to inclusive AI governance: learning from the past, co-building the future Date & Time:  ●7 July 2026, 12:00–12:45 (CEST) ●Room E (120) Organizers:  ●Organizers ○The Future Society     (TFS) ○Future of Life Institute     (FLI) ○The Elders     ○International Association for Safe and Ethical AI     (IASEAI) ○Global Network Initiative (GNI)     ○Centre for Communication Governance (CCG) at National Law University Delhi       (CCG) ○Multistakeholder Approaches to Participation in AI Governance     (MAP AI) ●Member State co-sponsors: ○Permanent Mission of Greece to the United Nations Office and other International  Organizations in Geneva ○Office of the Special Envoy on Technology for the Republic of Kenya Background and focus AI's cross-border impact demands both international coordination and genuinely inclusive multi- stakeholder engagement. The pace of frontier AI development outstrips the cycles through which  governments legislate, build institutions, and reach consensus. Its most significant risks cross   borders regardless of where systems are built; its benefits are concentrating among a few while  the effects are felt by all. No national framework, however sophisticated, can manage this alone. Meeting this moment requires something the international community has built before but must  now develop at speed: multilateral coordination grounded in geopolitical and socio-technical  realities, and meaningful multistakeholder engagement that draws in the wide range of expertise  this technology demands. This includes three essential constituencies. The Global Majority: advanced AI is a truly global  challenge, shaped by decisions made in a handful of jurisdictions yet affecting every country.  Frameworks built without those countries at the table will lack contextual relevance, legitimacy  and durability. The scientific and technical community: the technical risks of frontier AI are real  and specific, yet still poorly understood by many governance actors. Independent scientific  expertise must inform international processes, not follow them. And, civil society: the impact of AI  on society, the priorities of citizens and the scrutiny of independent organisations are not an  afterthought — they are an essential contribution to and condition of trustworthy governance. This side event convenes notable global leaders, technical experts, diplomats and civil society  representatives to look to the past to examine how international cooperation around other global  challenges was managed, and discuss how we co-build AI governance for the future. Drawing on  the first UN Global Dialogue and looking ahead to other key AI governance moments, it seeks to  map out how we can advance from learning to action: identifying key lessons, mapping viable  coordination pathways, and seeding the relationships needed to carry them forward. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6-7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    Driving Digital Inclusion in the Age of AI:   How Women and Countryside Communities Can Advance Responsible and Transformative AI     Date & Time: Tuesday, 7 July 2026, 07:00-08:30 CEST    Organizers:  Philippine ICT Innovation Network (PIIN) and the Digital Innovation for Women Advancement  (DIWA)    Short Title: The DIWA Dialogue  DIWA is a Filipino word that means spirit, essence, consciousness, or inner meaning.  For this dialogue, DIWA reflects the spirit of inclusive AI — where women, countryside communities, and local  innovators are not only included in the conversation but are empowered to shape the future of responsible and  transformative technology.    Background and focus  Artificial intelligence is reshaping work, enterprise, education, public services, and community development.  Its benefits will reach women and countryside communities only if inclusion is designed deliberately into  policies, infrastructure, skills programs, financing, and innovation ecosystems. For women, MSMEs, youth, and  communities outside major urban centers, AI can improve productivity, creativity, livelihoods, local problem- solving, and participation in the digital economy. Without purposeful action, however, AI may deepen gaps in  access, confidence, language, safety, data, finance, and representation.    This online side event will convene a focused dialogue on how responsible and transformative AI can advance  digital inclusion, especially for women and communities outside metropolitan centers. Drawing from Philippine  and Global South experience, it will highlight local ICT councils, digital jobs programs, startup and MSME  support, women-in-technology initiatives, and community-based innovation ecosystems. The discussion will  explore practical pathways for AI adoption that is human-centered, rights-respecting, culturally responsive,  and grounded in local needs.    The session will address three questions: How can women and countryside communities use AI for productivity  and digital-economy participation? What safeguards and governance principles are needed to build trust and  prevent exclusion, bias, and harm? How can governments, industry, academe, civil society, and local  innovation networks collaborate so AI becomes a bridge rather than a barrier? The expected outcome is a set of  actionable insights and partnership directions for inclusive AI capacity-building, responsible adoption, and  community-led innovation.    Speakers and Format  The 90-minute session will be an interactive policy and practice dialogue. It will open with brief framing remarks  by the Philippine ICT Innovation Network and Digital Innovation for Women Advancement (DIWA) advocates  on inclusive and responsible AI as a development strategy for women and countryside communities. This will  be followed by a moderated panel with perspectives from AI governance and digital inclusion, women in  technology, local innovation ecosystems, MSME/startup support, academe, and community-based ICT  development.         Proposed Flow: 5 minutes for welcome and objectives; 10 minutes for framing presentation; 40 minutes for  panel interventions; 20 minutes for moderated exchange with participants; and 15 minutes for synthesis, key  takeaways, and possible collaboration points. A Non-Resident  Fellow at the Dhirubhai Ambani School of Law, AI Policy Lead at RegHorizon,  Switzerland, and visiting faculty at leading Indian National Law Universities, her  research  spans  Constitutional  litigation,  Competition  law,  algorithmic  accountability,  arbitration  and  interoperability  mechanisms  for  global  AI  governance. Background and focus Artificial intelligence is being governed through a rapidly multiplying patchwork  of instruments: the EU AI Act and Digital Markets Act, Brazil’s draft AI framework  (PL 2338/2023), India’s emerging judicial and Ministerial sectoral guidance, the   Council of Europe Framework Convention, and a growing body of  soft-law  standards. This fragmentation creates two intertwined risks. First, compliance  burdens  concentrate  advantage  in  the  largest  firms  -  the  same  digital  gatekeepers whose market power AI now amplifies through control of compute,  foundation models, data, and distribution channels. Second, jurisdictions in the  Global South risk becoming rule-takers, importing frameworks calibrated to  other markets without the institutional capacity or interoperability mechanisms  needed to adapt them. This session merges two complementary proposals -  IBDI’s “AI Governance and  Digital Gatekeepers: Accountability, Interoperability and Market Power in the  European Union” (ID 79) and “From Fragmentation to Interoperability - Translator  Layers for Global AI Governance” (ID 85) - into a single conversation across the  European Union, Latin America, and South Asia. It examines (i) how EU-style  gatekeeper regulation addresses accountability and market power in AI value  chains, and what lessons and limits it holds for other regions; and (ii) whether  “translator layers” - technical, legal, and institutional mechanisms that map  obligations across regimes - can move global AI governance from fragmentation  to interoperability without forcing harmonization. Drawing on Brazilian, Indian, and European perspectives, speakers will explore  concrete design choices: mutual recognition of conformity assessments, model  documentation standards that travel across jurisdictions, interoperable audit  and incident-reporting formats, and the role of courts and regulators in the  Global South as active shapers rather than passive recipients of AI governance  norms. The objective is a set of actionable propositions for the Global Dialogue  on  how  accountability  for  powerful  AI  actors  and  interoperability  across  governance regimes can be pursued together rather than traded off against each  other. Speakers and Format The session will run for 45 minutes as a moderated roundtable designed for  interaction. Confirmed speakers: Dra. Alyne Andrade de Oliveira Bezerra (Director  of International Relations, IBDI) on EU gatekeeper regulation, digital markets,  and platform governance in the EU and Latin America; Ms. Nidhi Singh (Advocate- on-Record, Supreme Court of India) on translator layers, interoperability, and  algorithmic accountability from a Global South litigation and policy perspective;  and  Mr. Anurag Vijay (Advocate, Jharkhand High Court, India) on comparative  regulatory design and implementation in India.  Run of show: opening framing by the co-organizers (7 minutes); a moderated  exchange  structured  around  three  questions  -  who  is  accountable  for  AI  gatekeeper power, what would interoperability actually require, and what role   should the Global South play (23 minutes); open discussion with the audience (12  minutes); and closing takeaways for the Global Dialogue (3 minutes). The format  prioritizes dialogue over presentations: no slides, short interventions, and more  than a quarter of the session reserved for audience participation, reflecting the  co-equal collaboration between the organizing teams. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance 6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva Artificial Intelligence in Developing Countries: Opportunities,  Challenges, and Inclusive Governance Title: Artificial Intelligence in Developing Countries: Opportunities, Challenges, and  Inclusive Governance Date & Time:  6 July 2026, 07:00 PM – 07:45 PM CEST Organizers:  University of York Joining Link: https://us06web.zoom.us/j/87972178922? pwd=fk0GS97zgIMReO4x6dYey5vmffbtt6.1  A  short  description  (2–3  sentences)  for  the  public  programme  listing:  Artificial  intelligence  is  transforming  economies,  public  services,  and  societies  worldwide,  yet  many  developing countries continue to face significant barriers to its effective and responsible adoption. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    The Red Line Challenge  Global Convergence on AI Prohibitions      Date & Time:  7 July 2026, 19:00–20:00 CEST  Organizers:  Center for AI and Digital Policy  Format: Online panel discussion  Zoom registration link: https://us02web.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_1sIZlr1_TO-F3OHk9xSj0w  Short description for public program listing:  Enforcing prohibitions for AI systems incompatible with human rights and democratic values is a global  governance priority. Drawing on international AI frameworks and the CAIDP AI Index findings, the session  examines progress on AI prohibitions, focusing on progress, implementation gaps, and emerging issues.  Key questions include: Which AI systems are currently prohibited and how are these prohibitions  enforced? What new issues have emerged? How do we maintain momentum on implementation? Insights  can inform the UN International Scientific Panel and the Global Dialogue.  Background and focus  As AI systems become increasingly integrated into societies, governments face a fundamental governance  challenge: determining where clear red lines must be drawn to prevent AI uses that are incompatible with  human rights and democratic values. While global AI governance discussions have produced a growing  number of legal frameworks, an urgent question remains: are there circumstances where mitigation and  oversight are insufficient—and where certain AI applications should not be permitted?  Building on the Center for AI and Digital Policy’s (CAIDP) work on AI red lines and its CAIDP AI Index, this  session will explore the emerging global consensus that some AI uses require clear prohibitions. Across  international frameworks, including the UNESCO Recommendation on AI Ethics and the Universal  Guidelines for AI, national legislation, court decisions, and debates on military AI, governments and  institutions are increasingly recognizing that certain applications—including those involving mass  surveillance, social scoring, manipulative systems, discriminatory profiling, and AI systems that   undermine meaningful human control—pose risks that cannot be adequately addressed through technical  measures.  The session will examine how a human-centric approach can serve as the foundation for identifying AI red  lines. Rather than beginning with technological capabilities or existing mitigation tools, the discussion will  center on fundamental questions: What protects human dignity and agency? What safeguards equality,  democratic participation, and the rule of law?   Drawing from comparative insights across more than 90 countries through the CAIDP AI Index, the  session will examine progress in AI red lines, implementation gaps, and practical pathways for translating  principles into enforceable prohibitions. It will also consider how Global South governments and civil  society actors can shape AI governance debates as active participants in defining global norms.  The discussion will contribute to ongoing global AI governance efforts, including by providing insights  relevant to the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, and will support a shift from identifying  risks to advancing concrete governance action. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    A Path Toward International AI Governance:  Harmonizing Standards and Thresholds Across Jurisdictions      Date & Time:  06 July 2026, 17:00–17:45 CEST    Organizers:  French Center for AI Safety - CeSIA    Background and focus  This UN Global Dialogue side-event organized by the French Center for AI Safety (CeSIA) “A  Path Toward International AI Governance: Harmonizing Standards and Thresholds Across  Jurisdictions” directly contributes to Cluster 3 of the Global Dialogue, Safe, Secure and  Trustworthy AI: Interoperability and Compatibility of Approaches. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    Participation Without Power: Technology Sovereignty, Data Sovereignty and the  AI Divide in South Asia      Date & Time:  06 July 2026, 07:30 – 08:30 CEST     Organizers:  CODATA (Lead); Tribhuvan University; CSIR–National Institute Of Science  Communication and Policy Research (CSIR–NIScPR) ; DST Center for Policy Research – Indian  Institute of Science (DST- CPR IISc) ; UPES ; The Small Earth Nepal      Background and focus  South Asia's AI ambitions are clear. Across the region, governments are investing in AI  infrastructure, data platforms, and national strategies with the explicit goal of becoming builders,  not just consumers, of AI. Yet a structural tension sits unaddressed at the centre of this agenda. At  critical layers of the AI ecosystem, the infrastructure that powers these ambitions is operated  outside domestic jurisdiction, on terms governments did not set. The question this panel asks is  simple and unresolved: is South Asia building sovereign AI capacity, or deepening dependency in a  more sophisticated form?  The answer looks different depending on where you stand. India has invested significantly in AI  infrastructure and policy, yet structural dependencies persist. For countries with fewer resources,  the gap between ambition and ground reality is wider. For indigenous and tribal communities  across the region, the stakes are more immediate still. Their ecological knowledge, territorial  records, and oral traditions are entering AI systems without consent, across jurisdictions where no  single actor can be held accountable. Legal obligations under ILO Convention 169 and the UN  Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples exist. The current architecture makes them  difficult to enforce.  This panel brings together academics from India, Sri Lanka, and Nepal to examine four questions:  what is the current state of AI development in their countries; where dependency constrains  sovereign ambition; what governance conditions must exist before community data enters AI  pipelines; and what the international community must do differently to support sovereignty, not  just skills. The session is designed not to present consensus positions but to surface honest   accounts of where ambition meets ground reality, and where it does not, as a South Asian  contribution to the global AI governance agenda.      Speakers and Format  The panel brings together three academics with complementary expertise across AI governance,  law, and digital policy in South Asia.  Dr. Amit Kumar, Assistant Professor at the Research and Information System for Developing  Countries (RIS), New Delhi, brings expertise in technology assessment, AI governance, science  diplomacy, and the socio-economic implications of emerging technologies. His RIS Policy Brief on  AI and employment was cited in India's Economic Survey 2023-24.  Sahishnu Poudyal, Lecturer at Tribhuvan University and PhD Research Fellow at Kathmandu  University, contributes expertise in Media and Information Literacy, digital transformation, and  ethical AI governance. She coordinates the Research and Innovation workstream of the Women for  Ethical AI South Asia Chapter under UNESCO.  Dr. K. A. A. N. Thilakarathna, Senior Lecturer in Public and International Law at the Faculty of Law,  University of Colombo, brings expertise in the domestication of international human rights  obligations and the constitutional and regulatory implications of emerging technologies, with  growing research focus on algorithmic governance and digital rights.  Each speaker will offer opening remarks of 10 to 15 minutes drawing on their national context,  followed by a structured moderated exchange and an open Q&A session. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva     IAméricas: A roadmap towards Responsible AI      Date & Time:  06 July 2026, 17:00–17:45 CEST    Organizers: IAméricas, an initiative by Adigital and BID Lab, powered by fAIr LAC       Event Description  Adigital and BID Lab, through fAIr LAC, will present IAméricas, the initiative driving responsible AI  adoption among MSMEs and startups in Latin America and the Caribbean. The session, delivered  in Spanish, will offer a demonstrative introduction to the Responsible AI Organizational Maturity  Self-Assessment Framework, the tool that helps companies identify their starting point and  implement a roadmap toward responsible AI.  Background and focus  Artificial intelligence is no longer optional for Latin American MSMEs and startups: it is a condition  for competing. However, many organizations in the region still lack the frameworks, tools, and  support needed to adopt it responsibly and competitively. This session responds directly to that  gap.  Adigital and BID Lab, through fAIr LAC, present IAméricas, their joint initiative to drive the  responsible adoption of AI among MSMEs, startups, and innovation ecosystem stakeholders  across Latin America and the Caribbean. The project has already built a regional community of  more than 3000 participants and a network of implementation partners in Chile, Uruguay, Ecuador,  Mexico, Colombia, and soon Brazil, working toward concrete targets such as 1500 startups and  MSMEs adopting Responsible AI.  Participating in this event is relevant because it introduces attendees to one of IAméricas' core  tools: the Responsible AI Organizational Maturity Self-Assessment Framework, which helps  companies identify where they stand, based on criteria such as strategy, governance, risk  management, and training, among others, and implement a roadmap to strengthen their AI  governance.   The session, which will be delivered in Spanish, will open with a presentation of IAméricas and its  three components: awareness, training, and tools, followed by an awareness talk and an  interactive activity introducing the Self-Assessment Framework. Given the session's format, this  activity will be demonstrative: giving participants a clear sense of how the tool works and what kind  of insights they can gain from completing it.  The expected outcome is that each participant leaves with a clear understanding of what the self- assessment is, why it matters for their organization, and the motivation to join the formal process  to obtain their own diagnosis and roadmap.
