Actualmente el proyecto ya ha construido una comunidad regional de  más de 3000 participantes y una red de aliados de implementación en Chile, Uruguay, Ecuador,  México, Colombia y próximamente Brasil, avanzando hacia metas concretas como 1500 startups  y PyMEs que adoptan IA Responsable.  La participación en este evento es relevante porque acerca a los asistentes a una de las  herramientas centrales de IAméricas: el Marco de Autoevaluación de Madurez Organizativa en IA  Responsable, que ayuda a las empresas a identificar, a través de criterios como estrategia,  gobernanza, gestión de riesgos y formación entre otros, en qué punto se encuentran y a  implementar una hoja de ruta para fortalecer su gobernanza de IA.  La sesión, que será impartida en español, iniciará con una presentación de IAméricas y sus tres  componentes: sensibilización, formación y herramientas, seguida de una charla de sensibilización  y una actividad interactiva de acercamiento al Marco de Autoevaluación. Dado el formato de la   sesión, esta dinámica será demostrativa: dará a los participantes una idea clara de cómo funciona  la herramienta y qué tipo de información pueden obtener al completarla.  El resultado esperado es que cada participante salga con una comprensión clara de qué es la  autoevaluación, por qué le conviene a su organización, y con la motivación de sumarse al proceso  formal para obtener su propio diagnóstico y hoja de ruta. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    Empowering Vulnerable Voices: Human-Centric Safeguards in AI Governance      Date & Time:     06 July 2026, 13:30 - 14:10 CEST     Organizers:   LILY AI Safety Alliance - Melissa Pineda Brown -  AI Governance / Social Sciences Researcher; Lydia Thayline Gomes Da Conceição -  Founder / AI Safety Researcher / Activist, Daniel David - Technical Analyst / AI Safety Researcher.  Background and focus  As emerging technologies advance rapidly, their socio-cultural impacts on vulnerable populations remain deeply overlooked. This session  confronts the hidden crisis of algorithmic harms, specifically focusing on the rise of tech-facilitated misogyny, the silencing of female talent in  tech spaces, and severe psychological risks—such as emotional attachment to AI systems and its links to cyberbullying and self-harm among  youth. While global frameworks often treat AI safety as a purely technical baseline, the LILY AI Safety Alliance argues that true safety must be  intersectional and human-centric. Moving beyond theoretical policies, this discussion will present actionable solutions based on our published  Multilateral Governance Framework. We will explore the enforcement of gender-responsive "safety-by-design" principles, classify  non-consensual deepfakes as unacceptable risks, and advocate for the mandatory inclusion of diverse developers from the Global South. By  connecting technical vulnerabilities with real-world human rights, this session aims to build global coalitions to ensure that the future of artificial  intelligence protects and empowers half of the world’s population.  Speakers and Format  Lydia Thayline Gomes da Conceição (Brazil): Founder & Project Lead of the LILY AI Safety Alliance, independent cybersecurity researcher  specializing in AI Red Teaming, and grassroots activist from Rio de Janeiro advocating for vulnerable groups. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    Digital Public Goods and Societal AI Resilience: Bridging Capacity Gaps in the  Global Majority      Date & Time:  6 July 2026, 18:30–19:15 CEST    Organizers:  Policy Hub for Inclusive Development (PHID) · Olabi    Background and focus  Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping economies, public institutions, and societies  worldwide. While global AI governance discussions have made significant progress in  advancing principles related to safety, transparency, interoperability, and human rights,  implementation capacity remains highly uneven across countries. For many governments and  institutions in the Global Majority, the challenge is no longer simply accessing AI technologies,  but developing the institutional readiness required to govern, deploy, and benefit from AI  responsibly.  This session explores the role of Digital Public Goods (DPGs) as foundational infrastructure for  societal AI resilience. Open-source, interoperable, and reusable digital solutions can  strengthen public institutions, accelerate capacity-building, and reduce barriers to responsible  AI adoption. The discussion will examine how investments in shared digital infrastructure and  institutional capabilities can help countries move from AI access to AI readiness, while  equipping governments, communities, and younger generations to navigate an AI-driven  future.  Hosted by the Policy Hub for Inclusive Development (PHID) in collaboration with Olabi, the  session will take the form of an interactive fireside chat connecting practical experience with  global policy discussions. It will explore how governments, civil society, and international  organizations can leverage DPGs to strengthen public institutions, foster inclusive innovation,  and enhance international cooperation in support of effective, accountable, and inclusive  governance.  The discussion aims to contribute practical policy insights to the Global Dialogue on AI  Governance by highlighting scalable pathways for strengthening institutional capacity and   advancing more inclusive and resilient AI ecosystems across the Global Majority. Key  takeaways and recommendations from the discussion will be synthesized into a policy memo  to be shared with the Joint Secretariat and the Co-Chairs of the Global Dialogue on AI  Governance as a contribution from the session.  Speakers and Format  Format: Fireside Chat (45 minutes)  The discussion will be guided by the following questions:  ●​ How can DPGs help reduce inequalities in AI adoption across the Global Majority?  ●​ What are the main capacity and institutional challenges that countries in the Global  Majority face in preparing for the AI era?  ●​ Which experiences in majority countries demonstrate the potential of open digital  solutions to strengthen institutional capacity, foster inclusive innovation, and build  societal AI resilience?  ●​ How can digital inclusion and DPGs be more effectively integrated into the global AI  governance agenda?  Moderator  Michelle Perino, MPA (London School of Economics and Political Science), is Co-CEO of the  Policy Hub for Inclusive Development (PHID) and a specialist in poverty, inequality, and social  policy. Her work focuses on human rights, equality, and the design and implementation of  social policy programmes, advising governments, regulatory bodies, and private sector  organizations across Europe and Latin America. At PHID, she leads programme design and  delivery, connecting climate action, socioeconomic empowerment, and digital development to  advance inclusive and sustainable public policy solutions.  Speaker  Gabriela Agustini is Co-Executive Director and Co-Founder of Olabi, a Brazilian civil society  organization advancing digital inclusion, AI governance, and technological justice across the  Global South. An Ashoka Fellow, journalist, and researcher, she has spent more than a  decade designing initiatives that strengthen communities' agency in emerging technologies  through capacity building, participatory governance, open innovation, and public engagement.  Her work bridges technology, public policy, and social impact, with a particular focus on AI  governance, open-source ecosystems, and the inclusion of historically underrepresented  communities. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    Digital Safety Risks of Large Language Models (LLMs) and AI for Individuals with  Cognitive Disabilities and Neurodivergent Users      Date & Time: Monday, 6 July 2026 | 07:00–08:30 CEST    Organizers: Byomire Inclusive Development Foundation Ltd (BIDF) and Makerere University  Business School  Background and focus  Large Language Models (LLMs) and other Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are transforming  access to information, education, healthcare, employment, and digital participation. For many  persons with disabilities, these technologies offer unprecedented opportunities to improve  communication, independence, learning, and inclusion. However, despite growing global attention  to AI governance, the digital safety implications for persons with cognitive disabilities, intellectual  and developmental disabilities, and neurodivergent users remain largely overlooked. Individuals  with conditions such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder  (ADHD), and other cognitive or developmental disabilities may face unique challenges when  interacting with AI. These include difficulties in evaluating AI-generated information, recognizing  misinformation, identifying manipulation, protecting personal data, and responding appropriately  to unsafe or misleading content. Without adequate safeguards, AI systems risk reinforcing digital  exclusion and exposing vulnerable users to new forms of harm.  This session will examine key digital safety risks associated with LLMs, including misinformation,  manipulation, overreliance on AI-generated advice, unsafe prompting, privacy harms, algorithmic  bias, emotional dependency, and inaccessible safety features. It will also explore practical  approaches to disability-inclusive AI governance, including co-design with persons with  disabilities, accessible AI design, digital literacy, safeguarding frameworks, and institutional  accountability. Bringing together researchers, disability advocates, policymakers, AI governance  experts, and civil society representatives, the session will facilitate dialogue on how international  AI governance frameworks can better protect and empower vulnerable users. Drawing on emerging  research, lived experiences, and global policy developments, participants will identify actionable  recommendations for embedding disability inclusion and digital safety into AI governance.     The discussion contributes directly to the objectives of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance by  promoting AI systems that are safe, trustworthy, accessible, human-centered, and rights-based,  ensuring that no one is left behind in the age of artificial intelligence.  Speakers and Format  The session will be conducted as a 90-minute interactive online side event, combining expert  presentations, moderated discussion, and audience engagement.  Moderator: Gorretti Byomire  Co-Founder and Team Leader, Byomire Inclusive Development Foundation Ltd (Uganda)  Director, Disability Resource and Learning Centre, Makerere University Business School  Speaker  Dr. Hasifah Namatovu Kasujja  Lecturer, Department of Information Systems, Makerere University  Researcher in Artificial Intelligence, Human-Centered AI, and Digital Innovation  Invited Discussants  • Representative from a Disabled Persons' Organization (DPO)- Joel Kawanguzi (Persons  with Short Stature)  • AI governance and digital policy expert- Dorothy Ankunda (AI policy, governance, and  research)  • Civil society representative working on digital rights and safeguarding- Ruth Atim (Gender  Tech Initiative)  • Person with lived experience of neurodivergence or cognitive disability- Slyvia Nangabane   (Person living with Downs Syndrome)  The discussion will begin with brief presentations highlighting emerging evidence on digital safety  risks faced by persons with cognitive disabilities and neurodivergent users when interacting with  LLMs. A moderated panel will then explore governance gaps, inclusive AI design, safeguarding  approaches, and policy priorities. The session will conclude with an interactive question-and- answer segment and the development of practical recommendations for integrating disability- inclusive digital safety into national and international AI governance frameworks. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    From Users to Architects: A Co-authored Future with All Generations    Date & Time:  07 July 2026, 18:00–18:45 CEST    Organizers:   Lead: Geneva Hub | Young AI Leaders (YAIL)  Co-organizers:    Geneva Macro Labs / Geneva Network of Innovators (ge-ni),    Si Labs,    Youth AI Governance Forum (YAIGF),    YAIL Hubs coalition from Viseu, Bogotá, Zurich, Mexico City, Linz, Madrid, San  Francisco    Background and focus  We are excited to host The Hive’s high-level panel, “From Users to Architects: A Co- authored Future with All Generations” as part of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  online/offsite side-events programme. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    AI Governance for Development: A LAC Perspective      Date & Time:  7 July 2026, 08:15–08:45 CEST | Room E    Organizers:  Ministry of Science, Innovation, Technology and Telecommunications (MICITT) of  Costa Rica · Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) ·   Background and focus  Artificial intelligence is reshaping development pathways across Latin America and the Caribbean  (LAC), offering opportunities to accelerate productivity, innovation and public service delivery,  while also raising pressing questions on capacities, infrastructure, regulatory frameworks, human  rights and equitable access. As global discussions on AI governance advance, it is essential that  the region’s voice be clearly reflected in the emerging international architecture for AI governance.  This side event presents the outcomes of the AI4LAC Regional Dialogue, held on 26 May 2026,  which brought together government representatives, regional organizations and other stakeholders  from across LAC to articulate common positions, shared priorities and key messages on AI  governance ahead of the Global Dialogue. The synthesis note resulting from that process reflects  regional perspectives on issues such as building AI capacities and infrastructure, advancing  normative frameworks anchored in human rights, strengthening multilateral cooperation, and  positioning LAC strategically within global AI governance discussions.  The session aims to ensure that these regional positions are formally introduced into the  proceedings of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance, reinforcing LAC’s engagement in shaping a  global AI governance architecture that is inclusive, balanced and responsive to the development  needs of the region.  Speakers and Format  Given the 30-minute format of this side event, the session is structured around two concise  segments. Title: Approaches and Insights from the World’s Fastest AI-Adopting Economies
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    Approaches and Insights from the World’s Fastest AI-Adopting Economies       Date & Time:  07 July 2026, 12:45–13:30 CEST    Organizers:  Microsoft · Republic of Korea · Singapore · United Kingdom  Background and focus  Microsoft's AI Diffusion Reports reveal striking differences in how quickly countries are adopting  AI. The reason for tracking adoption specifically is that history demonstrates that value is not  necessarily captured by those who build a technology, but by those who adopt and diffuse it. As  with earlier general-purpose technologies, transformation comes from spread – the access,  infrastructure, skills, and enabling policies that let firms, governments, and citizens put AI to  work.    This event turns these insights into a practical conversation.     The Republic of Korea, Singapore and the UK, among the largest and fasting growing adopters of  AI in the world, will be sharing how their national strategies and approaches have translated into  real-world uptake, with the aim of sharing best practices, lessons learned, and where common  themes critical to enabling AI adoption.    Focus  • Practical lessons from the world's fastest adopters: Hear how they turned national  ambition into everyday use – through leadership in government, investment in skills, and  the right enabling conditions – in ways you can adapt to your own context.   • A conversation about closing the gap: Explore together how the conditions that drive  adoption can be extended to more countries, so that the benefits of AI reach all economies  and the divide between them narrows rather than widens.   • Common ground for working together: Identify where national approaches align, and  where greater cooperation and interoperability could make AI safer, more trusted and  easier to adopt across borders.    • A focus on shared benefit: See how wider, well-governed adoption of AI can accelerate  progress on the Sustainable Development Goals – ensuring AI works for people  everywhere.    Speakers and Format  This Panel will feature:  Microsoft - Natasha Crampton, Chief Responsible AI Officer (Moderator)     Microsoft – Kevin White, Senior Director, Data Science at Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab  Will share the latest details and insights from Microsoft’s AI Diffusion Report covering recent  trends including accelerating adoption in Asia driven by improving AI capabilities in Asian  languages and the data behind the widening digital divide.    Republic of Korea – H.E. Ambassador Jihoon Cha, Permanent Representative to the UN  Will share how the Republic of Korea became one of the world's fastest-growing AI nations -  through bold national leadership, major investment in computing power and chips, a  comprehensive Framework Act on Artificial Intelligence that balances trust with innovation, and a  deliberate effort to bring the benefits of AI into the daily lives of all citizens.    Singapore – Timothy Chin, Assistant Chief Executive, Infocomm Media Development  Authority  Will share Singapore’s experiences with implementing its National AI Strategy focused on the  public good, strong investment in skills and computing power, trusted AI testing tools, and  government leading the way as one of the world's most consistent adopters.    United Kingdom – Joe Carroll, Head of Artificial Intelligence Unit, UK Foreign,  Commonwealth and Development Office  Will share how the UK is becoming one of the world's leading AI nations - through its AI  Opportunities Action Plan and pioneering AI Safety Institute, pairing world-class research with a  pro-innovation approach to safety, and a drive to put AI to work across public services. Title: “Human Rights-Based AI Governance: Building Interoperable Frameworks
text_string: 1        CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva   “Human Rights-Based AI Governance: Building Interoperable Frameworks  through Transparency and Multistakeholder Participation”    Organisers: The Kingdom of the Netherlands; Peru; African Commission on Human  and Peoples’ Rights; Council of Europe; Centre for the Study of Law in Theory and  Practice, LJMU; Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI; Centre for Human Rights, University of  Pretoria, Global Centre for AI Governance    Format: Moderated multistakeholder discussion with interactive audience  participation    Background  This side event focuses on the fourth theme of the United Nations Global Dialogue on AI  Governance: "Respecting, protecting and promoting human rights: transparency, accountability  and human oversight."  It examines both the opportunities and risks that artificial intelligence presents for the  enjoyment and protection of human rights. The discussion will consider recent efforts to  strengthen human rights standards applicable to AI, with a particular focus on empowering  individuals and groups, especially vulnerable and marginalised communities.  The session will also explore how different regional human rights systems are responding to AI  governance, and how multistakeholder participation can be operationalised to support the  protection, promotion and fulfilment of human rights. It will consider the importance of  interoperability between governance approaches, while recognising regulatory diversity and  maintaining universal standards of human rights protection.  A central focus of the discussion will be the need to include all perspectives, including those  from underrepresented communities, so that interoperable AI governance reflects global  realities rather than a narrow set of perspectives. The session will also address the importance   2    of open data, transparency, accountability, human oversight and effective multistakeholder  mechanisms in protecting human rights in the age of AI.  Drawing on cross-continental and multistakeholder perspectives from co-organisers who have  led ground-breaking initiatives on AI and human rights, the session seeks to support the Global  Dialogue on AI Governance by identifying governance gaps, highlighting good practices, and  contributing to a human rights-centred approach to AI governance. In doing so, it also supports  the objectives of the Global Dialogue as set out in UN General Assembly Resolution  A/RES/79/325. text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    Artificial Insecurity: AI and Cybersecurity       Date & Time:  7 July 2026, 12:00–12:45 CEST     Organizers:  Access Now and Global Partners Digital (GPD)     Background and focus  300 words  This session brings together top experts from civil society, industry and government to explore how  cybersecurity and AI governance intersect. Looking beyond the hype, we propose a technically  grounded conversation on the cybersecurity implications of large language models and agentic AI.  Beyond just identifying risks, speakers will share concrete examples, challenge assumptions, and  discuss rights-respecting recommendations that strengthen security and public trust in advanced AI.     In particular, our discussion will focus on two topics: the impact of cutting edge AI tools on privacy and  encryption, as well as the threats and opportunities related to the use of AI tools for vulnerability  discovery in cybersecurity.    Regarding the impact of AI tools on privacy and encryption, questions to be asked include:  -​ What is the current state of the art regarding privacy and AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude etc?  What interests or rights are being prioritized and what risks are created for at-risk communities?  -​ How do developments in agentic AI threaten privacy, and even encrypted communications, and  what can be done to mitigate these risks?  -​ How does the integration of LLMs across digital services, such as search engines, platforms,  and messaging tools, create threats to the digital security of at-risk users and how could things  be done differently?    On the use of AI tools for vulnerability discovering, questions include:  -​ What lessons can we learn from the recent furore around cutting edge AI models being used to  discover security vulnerabilities? What can we put down to hype and what do we need to take  seriously?  -​ Access to these advanced models has been a key issue, with only a limited number of  stakeholders being given access to Anthropic’s Mythos model. How can we avoid a situation in  which robust security becomes dependent on privileged access to cutting edge AI models? Title: Parliamentary Oversight for Increased Transparency and Accountability of AI
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    Parliamentary Oversight for Increased Transparency and Accountability of AI      Date & Time:  Mon 6 July 2026, 14:15–15:00, Room E  Organizers:  Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) · Commonwealth Parliamentary Association (CPA) ·  United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)    Background and focus  The first Global Dialogue on AI Governance, mandated by General Assembly resolution 79/325, is  organised around four thematic clusters. The cluster on human rights, transparency,  accountability and human oversight raises a foundational question of how AI systems are governed  in democratic societies. Transparency, accountability and human oversight are core constitutional  functions of parliament, given effect through legislation that sets the rules, scrutiny of executive  action, public hearings and committee inquiries, budget oversight, and the protection of rights in  domestic law.    Parliaments have established a clear position on AI governance. The IPU resolution "The impact of  artificial intelligence on democracy, human rights and the rule of law" (149th IPU Assembly,  October 2024), the Kuala Lumpur Declaration on Parliaments and Responsible AI (November 2025,  adopted by parliamentary representatives from 65 countries), and the IPU motion on “Advancing  parliamentary action on artificial intelligence” (152nd IPU Assembly, Istanbul, April 2026) together  provide the basis for a substantive parliamentary mandate on AI governance and policy.    Parliamentary engagement in this area is emerging. While good practice is taking shape in different  regions, many parliaments lack the technical advisory infrastructure they need to legislate and  oversee AI effectively, and the gap is most acute for parliaments in the Global South. Parliaments  themselves have identified that they require expertise on the issues and representation in  international AI governance discussions. International discussion of AI capacity-building has  tended to focus on governments, with less attention to the key role of the legislative branch.    This workshop convenes parliamentarians from different regions to set out the parliamentary  mandate on transparency, accountability and oversight of AI; share concrete examples of the  impact parliaments are achieving; identify the support parliaments need; and consider how the   Global Dialogue and International Scientific Panel can help strengthen parliaments in their key  roles of legislating on AI, overseeing its deployment and representing the public interest.  Speakers and Format  The session is a workshop combining short case-study presentations from parliamentarians with  facilitated  peer  exchange,  designed  to  identify  practical  experience  and  concrete  recommendations for parliamentary action on transparency, accountability and oversight of AI.  Following a brief framing of the parliamentary mandate, speakers will present examples of action  from their parliaments:  • Senator Rojo Edwards (Chile) chairs the Senate Committee on Future Challenges, Science,  Technology and Innovation, and is a specialist in lawmaking and oversight of emerging  technologies.  • Hon. John Kiarie Waweru, MP (Kenya) chairs the National Assembly’s Committee on  Communication, Information and Innovation, which handles ICT, data-protection, and broader  digital-economy matters.  • Hon. Dina Al-Bashir, MP (Jordan) is a lawyer and member of the House of Representatives’ Legal  Committee, and has been active on AI governance, rule of law and human rights issues.   A facilitated discussion then considers what support parliaments need, and how Member States,  UN entities, civil society, academic and technical can help meet those needs. Title: Building Trust and Governance in the Era of Generative AI: Intellectual Property,
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    Building Trust and Governance in the Era of Generative AI: Intellectual Property,  Quality, Reliability and Accountability      Date & Time: Tuesday 7 July 2026, 12:45–13:30 CEST (45 minutes)    Organizers: Co-organised, co-equal collaboration: Russian Academy of National Economy and  Public Administration (RANEPA) and Ivannikov Institute for System Programming of the Russian  Academy of Sciences (ISP RAS), Russian Federation; with S.M for Intellectual Property (Egypt), an  intellectual-property and innovation advisory firm, and iPioneer, an AI–intellectual-property  governance and legal-technology platform (MENA region and the Global South).    Background and focus  As generative and multimodal AI systems move into public services, media, education, the creative  industries and the wider economy, two governance questions are converging. The first is whether  we can trust what these systems produce — how reliability, quality and robustness are measured  rather than merely asserted, and how such assessments can travel across borders. The second is  who is accountable for, and who holds rights over, AI outputs — how provenance, attribution and  intellectual-property frameworks keep pace with content that machines now generate at scale.  Both questions expose the same underlying gap: a shortage of shared, interoperable and  independently verifiable approaches. And both fall hardest on developing countries and emerging  regions that must assess and govern systems they did not build.  This session brings together two complementary communities of practice. One works on the  evaluation, verification and trust assessment of large language and multimodal models, combining  public-administration and systems-engineering expertise. The other works on intellectual property  and the broader legal, regulatory and governance dimension of AI — including AI governance, legal  capacity-building and the innovation ecosystems of startups and SMEs — with particular attention  to the MENA region and other developing economies. By placing reliability evaluation and  IP/provenance governance in the same conversation, the session moves from the abstract  principle of “trustworthy AI” toward concrete, comparable practices for measuring quality and for  establishing accountability and rights over AI-generated content.  The focus is deliberately practical and cross-regional. Speakers will compare how trust and rights  are handled in different jurisdictions, identify where frameworks diverge and where they can be   made interoperable without imposing a single rigid standard, and surface capacity-building needs  and partnership opportunities. The aim is to produce actionable input — captured in a short key- messages summary for the Joint Secretariat — that supports the constructive, equitable and  accountable development of AI worldwide.    Speakers and Format  Format. A 45-minute moderated panel designed for interaction and cross-regional exchange. A  single moderator — provided by the RANEPA side or, if preferred, a mutually agreed neutral  moderator — steers one integrated conversation so that technical-evaluation and  legal/intellectual-property perspectives respond directly to one another rather than running in  parallel. After a short framing, each panellist gives a brief opening position; the moderator then  threads shared questions across both themes, followed by an open audience Q&A and a closing  round of key messages. Delivered in English; no interpretation required.  Moderator. Dr. Pavel Golosov, Director of the Institute for Social Sciences, RANEPA.  Speakers. The panel brings together complementary expertise for a balanced, multidisciplinary  discussion. From the RANEPA side, the proposed list of speakers cover:   -  Ms. Oksana Sotnikova, Director of the Department of Strategic Development and  Innovation, Ministry of Economic Development of the Russian Federation — AI policy and  the governance of AI research and intellectual property;   -  Dr. Arutyun Avetisian, ISP RAS Evaluation, — verification & trust assessment of AI systems;  -  Mr. Dmitry Ontoev, Department of Information Technology of the City of Moscow — AI in  smart cities and the digitalisation of urban governance;   -  Mr. Alexey Shpilman, Director for AI Technology Development, T-Technologies — AI in  cybersecurity.   From the intellectual-property side:  -  Ms. Shrouk Abdelaziz, Founder & CEO of S.M for Intellectual Property and Founder of  iPioneer — AI governance and intellectual property from a regional and practical perspective  (MENA and the Global South);  -  Further speakers — covering international intellectual-property law and governance and,  where feasible, AI governance and public policy from an international perspective — are  being finalised. Title: CISG Smart Contracts: AI Governance and Trade
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    CISG Smart Contracts: AI Governance and Trade      Date & Time:  Tuesday 7 July 2026, 12:45–13:30 CEST, Room G    Organizers:  Tecnológico de Monterrey    Background and focus  Artificial intelligence is transforming international trade by supporting the drafting, analysis, and  execution of commercial agreements. While these technologies improve efficiency and  automation, they also raise governance questions regarding legal compliance, accountability,  transparency, and the role of human oversight. In legally sensitive domains such as international  commercial contracting, technological innovation alone is insufficient. Effective AI governance  therefore requires appropriate legal frameworks and meaningful human oversight throughout the  AI-assisted decision-making process.   This session presents research on the development and validation of an artificial intelligence (AI)  system trained on the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods  (CISG) to assist in drafting legally compliant international sales contracts and translating them into  executable blockchain smart contracts. The study demonstrates the feasibility of using AI to  support legally compliant contract drafting and smart contract generation while revealing both the  opportunities and limitations of AI-assisted legal contracting. Although the AI system automated  substantial aspects of contract drafting and smart contract generation, it could not independently  perform complex legal reasoning, regulatory interpretation, contractual negotiations, dispute  resolution, financial verification, or legal enforcement, demonstrating that human expertise and  institutional oversight remain indispensable.   Building on these findings, the session examines their implications for AI governance in  international trade by addressing a central question: Can AI independently support the complete  lifecycle of international legal contracting? Drawing on this case study, the session argues that  effective AI-assisted legal contracting continues to depend on legal frameworks, human expertise,  financial institutions, arbitration mechanisms, and judicial enforcement working alongside AI  systems. The session concludes by presenting a preliminary discussion framework that organizes   these legal, institutional, and human oversight mechanisms to support future international  discussions on responsible AI governance for AI-assisted legal contracting.    Speakers and Format  The session will be presented by Hatem Mabrouk, Professor of International Business at  Tecnológico de Monterrey. His research focuses on international trade law, blockchain  technologies, artificial intelligence, and AI governance, with particular emphasis on the application  of emerging technologies to international business law. The presentation is based on recent  research examining whether an AI system trained on the United Nations Convention on Contracts  for the International Sale of Goods (CISG) can draft legally compliant international sales contracts  and translate them into blockchain smart contracts while identifying the practical and legal  limitations of AI-assisted legal contracting.   The session will be delivered as an expert presentation followed by a moderated discussion with  participants. It will present the research methodology, principal findings, and governance  implications while encouraging dialogue among policymakers, legal practitioners, researchers,  industry representatives, and technology experts. Participants will be invited to exchange  perspectives on the opportunities and limitations of AI-assisted legal contracting and on the legal,  institutional, and human oversight mechanisms that remain essential for responsible AI  governance. Title: From AI Governance Evidence to Local Readiness: Prototyping Public-Interest
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE    First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    From AI Governance Evidence to Local Readiness: Prototyping Public-Interest  AI through Intercultural Dialogue      Date & Time:  Mon 6 Jul, 14:15–15:00 CEST    Organizers:  Global Center on AI Governance, BRISD, EuroMedAI    Background and focus  300 words  The goal of ensuring societies benefit from AI while preventing its potential harms has become a  recurring commitment across global fora, international agreements, and national policy initiatives.  Yet these commitments do not guarantee that AI will improve people’s lives, especially at the local  level where public services, civic participation, and social inclusion are directly experienced.  Translating principles into action raises critical questions: What are the most pressing AI  governance challenges? Where are countries and regions making progress? How can global  evidence inform local AI readiness? And how can intercultural dialogue help build governance  frameworks that reflect regional legal traditions, civic cultures, linguistic diversity, and community  needs?   This session brings together three organizations tracing a path from AI governance evidence to local  readiness, through intercultural exchange and prototyping.  The Global Index on Responsible AI (GIRAI), developed by GCG, compiles first-hand data from 130+  countries examining national commitments, institutional capacity, and policy implementation.  Built through a research network rooted in the Global Majority, GIRAI reflects a core premise: global  findings must be grounded in local evidence. GCG will share initial insights and reflect on the  challenges of capturing diverse local perspectives — voices too often absent from policy debates.  EuroMedAI contributes a Mediterranean perspective on translating global AI governance evidence  into local readiness. Building on its AI maturity assessment of the South Mediterranean, EuroMedAI  works with regional stakeholders to develop an AI governance readiness framework for local  governments in the South Mediterranean. The session will be an opportunity to present an initial  roadmap of the framework, invite feedback from participants, and explore how intercultural   dialogue can help adapt global AI principles to regional legal traditions, civic cultures, and  community needs.  BRISD focuses on youth and professionals from the Global South directly affected by AI decisions  but rarely represented in policy spaces. Through prototyping, participants analyze governance  challenges from their own countries using accessible AI tools and assess what those tools capture  — and what they miss.    Speakers  ● Nicolás Grossman - Global Center on Ai Governance: Nicolás Grossman is the Project  Director of the Global Index on Responsible AI at the Global Center on AI Governance  (GCG). He is a sociologist and journalist with extensive experience leading global research  initiatives focused on data for the public good and responsible AI.  ● Mohamed ALOUANE — EuroMedAI: Mohamed is a Development Program Specialist and  civil society expert with over a decade of experience driving impact across the  Mediterranean region. His work centers on advancing theories of change within key areas  such as democratic governance, inclusive economic growth, AI governance, and digital  inclusion.  ● BRISD —Imran khan — BRISD: Imran Khan is a computer engineer and AI practitioner,  implementing artificial intelligence systems across industry. He serves as Director of AI  Safety and Technical Governance at BRISD, where he leads work on responsible AI  development, algorithmic accountability, and governance frameworks for emerging  technologies. Imran is also a certified AWS PartyRock Educator, recognised by Amazon for  his commitment to democratising AI literacy and empowering the next generation of  practitioners and policymakers.   Format  The session runs for 45 minutes and follows a structured three-part format.  ● Welcome and agenda (6 min) — Brief welcome and session framing by the co-organizing  partners.  ● Presentations (33 min) — Each organization delivers an 11-minute presentation. GCG  opens with evidence and initial insights from GIRAI; EuroMedAI follows with the  intercultural and local governance perspective; BRISD closes with a participatory  prototyping demonstration, drawing on pre-session work with a small group of participants  who will have engaged with the AI policy tool in advance.  ● Closing reflection (5 min) — Moderator-led synthesis and key takeaways. Title: Children are rights-holders under the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history - the
text_string: Co-sponsored by France, Spain, the EU, Kenya Side-event – Joining efforts for Children’s Rights and Protection  in the Age of Artificial Intelligence Tuesday 7 July, 12.45-13.30 – Room K Concept note and run of show 1. Context     Children are rights-holders under the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history - the  Convention on the Rights of the Child - yet AI governance frameworks have largely treated them as an  afterthought: a vulnerable sub-group requiring protection, rather than full rights-holders entitled to  participation, access, non-discrimination, and redress.  Children are also the clearest test of whether  global AI governance can translate principles into practice. If governance frameworks cannot stop the  proliferation of AI-generated child sexual abuse material, prevent algorithmic discrimination in welfare  and justice systems, protect children's sensitive personal data, and close the access gap so that no  children are left behind, as well as enable their meaningful participation in decisions that affect them,  they will not deliver for anyone. Many of the emerging risks for children (including deepfake-enabled exploitation, harmful content  amplification and manipulative chatbots) are driven by generative and adaptive AI systems, whose  rapid deployment outpaces the safeguards currently in place for child-facing services. Safe-by-design  approaches and responsible AI practices are therefore increasingly critical considerations in addressing  AI-related risks for children. Over the past months, children’s rights and protection in the age of AI have been central to a growing  number of national and regional jurisdictions’ considerations on AI governance. These issues have also  been at the forefront of recent multilateral discussions, including the Africa Forward Summit (Nairobi,  11-12 May) and the French G7 presidency which culminated with the Evian Summit (15-17 June). For many countries, and across Africa in particular, the question is also one of equitable participation in  the age of AI. Children are among the fastest-growing users of digital technologies, but they are often  served by systems that do not reflect their languages, cultures, contexts, protection needs, or public  education realities. This makes children's rights in AI not only a safety concern, but also a question of  inclusion, digital sovereignty, public-interest innovation, and development. The first Global Dialogue on AI Governance offers an opportunity for all Member states, UN entities and  all stakeholders committed to ensure that the development and deployment of artificial intelligence  upholds the safety, healthy development and rights of every child to join forces through the launch of a  Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. 2. Objectives     As children’s rights and protection in the age of AI spans across all four pillars of the Dialogue, the  proposed side-events aims at identifying areas of focus and existing initiatives or commitments that  could feed into an actionable roadmap for members of the Coalition, to be designed following the  Geneva Dialogue. The Coalition should also identify practical areas for pilot cooperation, including child rights impact  assessments,  AI  safety  guidance  for  schools,  capacity-building  for  child  protection  institutions,  multilingual and culturally grounded AI tools, mechanisms for reporting and responding to AI-enabled   Co-sponsored by France, Spain, the EU, Kenya harms affecting children, strengthening coordination among all stakeholders; and enhancing best- practice sharing (including through the Independent Scientific Panel on AI). Below are some guiding questions that could help frame interventions in this regard: Cluster 1 (opportunities and implications): Where are the documented opportunities of AI for children,  in education, health, child protection and accessibility, and how can global norms support their  equitable diffusion rather than commercial capture of public services? How can AI systems better  support children’s rights and well-being across different contexts, while addressing the specific risks  that may arise in AI mediated environments? Cluster 2 (bridging divides): What would a children's dimension to AI and data sovereignty look like in  practice; what responsibilities should AI developers bear for linguistic and cultural inclusion and how  can capacity-building reach the educators and caregivers who shape children's AI exposure? How can  AI systems used by children be designed for linguistic diversity, local content, disability inclusion, and  African cultural contexts, and how can public digital infrastructure support safe and equitable access  for learners, educators, parents, and caregivers? Cluster 3 (safe, secure, trustworthy AI): What interoperable standards would address the AI-generated  child sexual abuse material (CSAM) crisis, the rise of harmful direct-to-consumer chatbots, and the  under-regulated risks of anthropomorphism and substitution in systems used by children? How can AI,  trusted data systems, and  responsible  public mobilization strengthen national child  protection  systems, including efforts to identify missing children, detect online exploitation, support referral  pathways, and improve coordination between families, schools, platforms, law enforcement, and child  protection agencies?  Cluster 4 (human rights, transparency, accountability): What governance mechanisms - including child  rights impact assessment, independent benchmarking of AI systems against child rights standards, and  binding algorithmic transparency requirements and technical safeguards in child-facing services - are  needed to make accountability verifiable rather than aspirational, and how can meaningful child  participation be embedded in these frameworks? 3. Title: The Algorithms That Bedevil African AI Workers
text_string: CONCEPT NOTE  First Session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance  6–7 July 2026 I Palexpo, Geneva    The Algorithms That Bedevil African AI Workers    Date & Time:  Monday 6 July 2026, 13:30–14:15 CEST · Room G (capacity 100) · Event P-7 (ID 260)    Organizers:  Africa AI Policy Lab (Lawyers Hub), lead · London School of Economics and Political Science · International Labour  Organization · Kenya Union of Gig Workers (KUGWO) · Macmillan Keck, Attorneys & Solicitors · Government of India (IndiaAI)  Background and focus  African data labellers, content moderators, and platform workers train and maintain the systems the world now calls artificial  intelligence. They sit at the base of the global AI supply chain and work under algorithmic management they cannot see, query, or  contest. Documented cases across the continent show sub-poverty pay, traumatic exposure to harmful content, and accounts  deactivated by automated systems without human review or recourse. When scrutiny rises in one jurisdiction, the work moves to  another, and the platform-as-contractor model keeps the firm at arm’s length from any duty of care.  The ground shifted in June 2026, when the International Labour Conference adopted Convention No. 193 on decent work in the  platform economy, the first binding international standard written for this work. It covers platform workers whether or not they hold  an employment relationship, sets safeguards on algorithmic management and on suspension and deactivation, ties employment status  to factual reality and not to contract wording, and pulls intermediaries and cross-border operators inside its scope. The standard now  exists. African ratification and the national measures that turn text into protection do not yet, and that gap is where this session works.
